To a Daughter at School.

DEAR ROSALIE:—Your improvement in some branches is good, but you have acquired bad habits of pronouncing some words which is barbarism, and the use of certain phrases which is very vulgar. During your vacation, several lapses dropped from your lips, which have resonated, and now allow you to look into the end.

You never used such phrases at home, prior to last winter; hence I infer two defects: that in that famed Academy good many keen young ladies are your companions, and your teacher is not sufficiently strict to correct your very awkward manner in these things.

Your errors in Grammar are intolerable.

Got. "I've got my lesson, dinner, hat, Satchel, &c." I got to see her just as she was starting &c. "Have," as a verb, implies possession, and is more elegant than "I've got." "Have learned" or "committed my lesson." "Was allowed to see her," or "make her visit official." "Went." "She hadn't ought to have went." Several errors in this. She ought not to have gone.

"Intended to have wrote." This is in one of your late letters! But the past infinitive cannot be connected, grammatically, with a verb expressing intention. "Intended to write" is correct; but intention to do a thing must be joined to the present infinitive.

Set. "She set down"—"she set on the chair." "Sat" is the past tense of "sit." The verb "set" is active transitive; "he set post," or "set on tree" is proper.

Lay. "She laid on the sofa or bed." "Lay" is the past tense of "lie," the verb you ought to employ; we can say "she laid herself on the cold ground;" but "he lay all night on the Battle field" is correct.

Eat. "She eat her breakfast." "Ate" is the past tense, not "eat"; "eat" is Latin conjugation.

Done. "She done it." Do, did, done. "Done" is the participle, and wrong. Break, broke, broken; but you would not say, "she broken it." Do, did, have done.

Fix. "I'm fixing to go." To "fix" is to fasten, to make permanent, but fastening to go, is contrivance. To "fix" post, and speak of fixtures; to "fitting," arranging, or preparing to go, is proper.

See. "Our sister says you used this word, 'I seed her do it,'" but this astounds me, and shows how prolific and contagious are bad habits and illiterate associates.

Learn. "The principal learns me Arithmetic." The teacher teaches,—the pupil learns. No scholar uses "learn" in this way.

Them. "Them trees, them books." "Them" is a personal, not adjective pronoun: hence cannot qualify nouns; "those trees, books, houses, &c.," is proper.

Like do. "All the girls do like do." "Like" may govern an accusation, but cannot precede nomination in this sentence. The girls do as do, or act like me; but not "like do."

I am in blushes, you may be certain as I record these errors, but it is better that you be corrected now, than to wait till your own school, which I hope will commence in a year or two, shall detect them. What could you exhibit before a class of young ladies if you had in the hurry of the moment, allowed some of the above expressions to escape you?

They would be all in a litter, and you would never forget it.

Then you have contracted a bad habit of pronouncing that is horrible: you make long and narrow where it ought to be broad; "was," "is," "has," "passed," "can't," etc.—Though I have frequently corrected the expression, you yet use "I am mistaken" &c., when this is far from your meaning. "She is mistaken when she says the Ganges runs through Ireland." No, she mistakes—she is in error—does not know Geography: mistake, mistook, mistaken. One may mistake her expressions, especially if her enunciation was indistinct: but cannot affirm "she is mistaken in regard to the Ganges"; she is ignorant, she mistakes the meaning or the words of the author.

That long, that high, that big, &c., sometimes escapes our ears, but the habit is not confirmed of using "that" for "so" long, high, big, &c.

How could you, this side Mason & Dixon's line, contract the use of "onto" so glibly? "She got onto the horse," fence! real Yankeeism. Barbarous as it is, it has crept into some books printed "down East."

Your affectionate Father,

S. A.

the copper mines of Lake Superior form an
exception to the general laws of mining oper-

regarded as a sort of accident of mines, and
not, by any means, to be relied on as a per
manent source of the metal. In our lake
region, however, the copper is diffuse through
the rocks, not in the State of ore, but as pure
malleable metal. Scattered among the great
masses of copper are found little shots or
pockets of silver. These have usually been
stolen by the miners in their underground
workings, so that comparatively little has
found its way to the proprietors of the mines.

It was generally believed, until lately, that
the silver was confined to the shots and peck
ets alluded to, and that the great masses of
copper contained at most, an unappreciable
quantity of the more valuable metal. Some,
however, dissented from this opinion, and,
among others, Truman Smith made himself

neglect.

Of late, however, attention has again been
attracted to the silver in Lake Superior cop-
per. The richness of this metal is now in
danger of being as much overestimated as it
has been recently moderated. We hear
marvellous stories of the productiveness of
